Q: What is the best practice to create a unique url for every user profile A:

Try to Use a simple, readable and unique structure. Avoid random messy strings. Preferred URL Formats

/user/john-doe /

profile/john-doe-123

/u/john-doe

Main Ways to Make an Account Unique

Username-based URL Use the username chosen by the user

Lowercase & replace spaces with hyphens

Example: John Doe john-doe

Add a unique identifier

Prevent duplicates by adding a number or ID

Example: john-doe-4578

Use database ID (secure option)

Example: /user/45821

Or combine: /john-doe-45821

Q: How do I debug a webhook POST? A:

I see some solid suggestions above like ngrok and RequestBin

This is a pretty old thread, but I still wanted to share something in case it helps, cause this is a problem pretty much everyone runs into at some point when dealing with webhooks

In practice, the most effective approach is to work in a loop: capture → inspect → replay.

Seeing the real request in real time helps catch common issues (like an unexpected content-type), and being able to replay it avoids having to manually trigger it from the provider each time.

For local development, a CLI with tunneling is usually the simplest option, i recommend:

npx @eventpipe/cli listen your-webhook-id  --forward-to http://localhost:8000/handler.php

This lets you receive webhooks and forward them to your local environment without exposing your machine directly.

I’ve been working on this small CLI/platform to solve this exact workflow (trying to combining the best parts of different tools). It includes:

  • A real-time request inspector (where you can get your-webhook-id)

  • A CLI to forward traffic to your localhost

  • And something we built called Pipe Studio, which lets you automate flows based on your webhooks

In case anyone wants to check it out: https://eventpipe.app/

Q: How to learn SQL? A:

Have you learned a second or third language in school? Then it's similar to that, but much easier because most computer languages have a relatively simple grammar compared to most spoken and written languages (no tenses, no pronouns, etc). And a lot less words, whose spelling doesn't differ between regions or between spoken and written.

The main problem with SQL is that it requires a different way of thinking compared to most other computer languages. Also there are many dialects of SQL, where the basic statements are similar enough to make it easy to switch between the dialects, to big differences (mostly for procedures and such, which are very specific to every database engine).

And you really learn it bit by bit, starting from the simplest parts and add the more complex parts as you get more experience. Just like anything else you need to learn.
